guide.title: Unit 2: Selection and Iteration: review guide
guide.intro: This unit covers how programs make decisions and repeat work: Boolean expressions, if statements, while and for loops, and the standard algorithms built from them. It carries a large share of the multiple-choice section. Trace code by hand, writing down each variable's value after every step.

sections.title: Boolean expressions and if statements
body: Algorithms are built from sequencing, selection, and repetition. The relational operators ==, !=, <, >, <=, and >= produce Boolean values. With primitives, == compares values; with references, it compares whether two variables refer to the same object.

An if statement runs its body only when its condition is true; if-else chooses between two bodies. In a multiway if-else-if chain, conditions are tested in order and only the body for the first true condition runs. Separate if statements are each tested, so more than one body can run. A nested if is evaluated only when the outer condition is true.
points: else-if chain: at most one branch runs; separate ifs: each is tested.
An else belongs to the nearest unmatched if in the same block.

sections.title: Compound and equivalent Boolean expressions
body: The logical operators are ! (not), && (and), and || (or); ! is applied first, then &&, then ||. Evaluation short-circuits: in a && b, b is not evaluated when a is false, and in a || b, b is not evaluated when a is true. This lets a test such as n != 0 && 10 / n > 2 avoid dividing by zero.

Two Boolean expressions are equivalent when they have the same value in every case, which a truth table can show. De Morgan's laws: !(a && b) is equivalent to !a || !b, and !(a || b) is equivalent to !a && !b. Negating a comparison flips it: !(x < 5) is x >= 5. Object references can be compared with == and != (including with null); equals compares objects by the criteria their class defines.
points: Not (A and B) = (not A) or (not B).
Put the safety check first so short-circuiting protects the second test.

sections.title: while and for loops
body: A while loop tests its condition before each iteration, including the first, so its body may run zero times. If the condition never becomes false, the loop is infinite. An off-by-one error makes a loop run one time too many or too few.

A for loop header has an initialization (run once), a condition (tested before each iteration), and an update (run after each iteration). Any for loop can be rewritten as a while loop and vice versa: put the initialization before the loop and the update at the end of the body.
points: for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) runs n times.
Check a loop's first value, last value, and the value that ends it.

sections.title: Loop algorithms, nested loops, and run-time
body: Standard algorithms: test divisibility with % (n % d == 0); take digits off an int with n % 10 and n / 10; count how often a condition is met; find a minimum or maximum; compute a sum or average. Standard string algorithms use a loop with substring to examine each character, count substrings with a property, or build a reversed string.

With nested loops, the inner loop runs completely for each iteration of the outer loop. A statement execution count is the number of times a statement runs; find it by tracing. If the inner loop's bounds depend on the outer variable, add up the inner counts (for example 1 + 2 + 3).
points: Last digit: n % 10; remove it: n / 10.
Outer loop n times and inner loop m times: the inner body runs n × m times.

example.prompt: How many times is the statement count++ executed?  for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) { for (int j = 0; j < i; j++) { count++; } }
example.solution: The inner loop runs i times for each i: 0 times when i is 0, then 1, 2, and 3 times. The total is 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 6.

misconceptions: “In an if-else-if chain, every true condition's body runs.”
Only the body for the first true condition runs.
By De Morgan's law it is !a || !b.
“A while loop always runs at least once.”
Its condition is tested first, so the body may never run.
“== compares the contents of two strings.”
== compares references; use equals to compare contents.

questions.prompt: The int variable x has the value 6. What is printed by the statement  System.out.println((x > 2 && x < 5) + " " + (x > 2 || x < 5));  ?
questions.explanation: x > 2 is true and x < 5 is false. && needs both to be true (false); || needs at least one (true).
choiceExplanations: This reverses the two results.
&& is true only when both parts are true, and 6 < 5 is false.
|| is true when at least one part is true, and 6 > 2 is true.

questions.prompt: For boolean variables a and b, which expression is equivalent to  !(a && b)  for all values of a and b?
questions.explanation: De Morgan's law: negating an and gives the or of the negations.
choiceExplanations: !(a || b) is true only when both are false; !(a && b) is also true when just one is false.
a || b is true when both are true, but !(a && b) is false then.
!a && !b is equivalent to !(a || b); it differs when exactly one of a and b is true.

> and < leave out the endpoints 2000 and 2025.
With ||, every year satisfies at least one condition, so this is always true.

questions.prompt: The code segment is intended to print 01234. What is wrong with it?
choices: The loop prints 12345, because i should start at the value 1.
The loop stops too early, because the condition should be i <= 5.
The loop never ends, because i is never changed inside the loop.
The loop never runs, because the condition i < 5 starts out false.
questions.explanation: i stays 0, so i < 5 is always true: an infinite loop that prints 0 repeatedly. Adding i++ inside the body fixes it.
choiceExplanations: i starts at 0 and never changes, so 1 through 5 are never printed.
The loop does not stop at all; changing the bound would not fix the missing update.
0 < 5 is true, so the loop does run.
